name: Second law of thermodynamics
kicker: Heat flows hot to cold on its own · Entropy never falls in an isolated system
briefing: The second law of thermodynamics explains why hot cocoa cools down and ice melts in a warm room, but never the other way around: heat flows on its own from hot things to cold things, unless something does work to push it back. Another way to say it is that entropy, a measure of disorder, never decreases in an isolated system. It also means no engine can turn all of its heat into useful work, so even the best engine wastes some heat.
answerHtml: Second law of thermodynamics (accept 2nd law of thermodynamics; prompt on second law or thermodynamics; do not accept “entropy” or another law)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures,” C. P. Snow said that being unable to describe this law was like never having read a work of Shakespeare. Arthur Eddington wrote that this law holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: A ship that ran by pulling heat out of the ocean and turning all of it into work would obey the conservation of energy but break this law. Lord Kelvin and Max Planck each gave a version of this law about engines like that one.
tossups.r: That version says no engine working in a cycle can turn heat entirely into work. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Refrigerators and air conditioners do not break this law, because they use electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space into a warmer room. Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] published a famous statement of this law in 1854.
tossups.r: That statement says heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics.

tossups.p: Sadi Carnot [“kar-NOH”] laid groundwork for this law in his 1824 book _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_, which argued that a heat engine must always pass some heat on to a colder body. The most efficient possible engine runs on a cycle named for Carnot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no heat engine can be 100 percent efficient.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell imagined a tiny “demon” that sorts fast and slow gas molecules between two boxes, which would seem to break this law by making one box hot and the other cold without doing any work. Physicists later showed that the demon’s need to record and erase information about the molecules would save this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Ludwig Boltzmann [“BOHLTS-mahn”] explained this law with statistics: disordered arrangements of molecules vastly outnumber orderly ones, so a system almost always drifts toward disorder. This law gives time a one-way direction that Arthur Eddington called the “arrow of time.”
tossups.r: It explains why ice melts in a warm room. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy tends to increase.

tossups.p: In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether the effects of this law on the whole universe can ever be undone. Applied to the universe, this law suggests a far-future “heat death,” with no temperature differences left to power anything.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which explains why heat flows from hot objects to cold ones.

tossups.p: Erwin Schrödinger’s [“SHROH-ding-erz”] 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored how living things stay organized despite this law. A living cell can lower the disorder inside itself only by giving off heat that raises the disorder of its surroundings even more, so life never breaks this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: In a joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics, the first law says “you can’t win” and this law says “you can’t break even.” This law explains why a car engine must waste some of the energy in its fuel as heat.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which also says that heat flows on its own only from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1865, Rudolf Clausius [“KLOW-zee-us”] summed up thermodynamics in two rules, saying that the energy of the universe is constant and that its entropy tends toward a maximum. That same year, Clausius gave entropy its name.
tossups.r: The rule about entropy is this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: When the wall between a box of gas and an empty box is removed, the gas spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one, as this law predicts. The chance of all the molecules gathering back in one box by accident is so tiny that it never happens in practice.
tossups.r: Hot cocoa cools to room temperature because of this law. For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

tossups.p: Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on this law. This law sets the best possible efficiency of a heat engine at one minus the ratio of its cold temperature to its hot temperature, measured in kelvins.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that entropy never decreases in an isolated system.

tossups.p: Jacob Bekenstein [“BEK-en-stine”] proposed a “generalized” version of this law that counts the entropy of black holes along with ordinary entropy. Stephen Hawking at first doubted Bekenstein, but then showed that black holes give off radiation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that the total entropy of an isolated system never goes down.

tossups.p: A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal without breaking this law, because the heat it gives off as it freezes raises the disorder of the air around it even more. Ice cubes can form in a freezer for a similar reason, since the freezer dumps even more heat into the kitchen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says heat flows on its own from hot to cold.

tossups.p: In 1851, William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, stated this law as the rule that no machine can get useful work out of an object just by cooling it below the temperature of its coldest surroundings. A perpetual-motion machine that kept running by recycling its own heat would break this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this law of thermodynamics, which says that no engine can be 100 percent efficient.

clues.t: Heat flows on its own from hot objects to cold ones, never the reverse, unless something does work to push it
The entropy (disorder) of an isolated system never decreases
No heat engine can be 100 percent efficient; some heat is always wasted
Explains why hot cocoa cools to room temperature and ice melts in a warm room, but never the reverse
Rudolf Clausius laid its foundation in 1850; his 1854 statement: heat cannot pass on its own from a colder body to a warmer one
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), 1851: no machine can get work out of an object just by cooling it below its coldest surroundings
Kelvin–Planck statement: no engine working in a cycle can turn heat from one source completely into work
Refrigerators and air conditioners obey it by using electrical work to pump heat out of a cold space
Sadi Carnot’s 1824 _Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire_ laid its groundwork; the Carnot cycle is the most efficient possible engine
Joke summary of the laws of thermodynamics: the first says “you can’t win,” and this one says “you can’t break even”
The first law says energy is conserved; this one says which way energy naturally flows
Applied to the whole universe, it suggests a far-future “heat death” with no temperature differences left
Maxwell’s demon, an imaginary molecule-sorter, seemed to break it; the cost of recording and erasing the demon’s information saves it
C. P. Snow’s 1959 lecture “The Two Cultures”: not being able to describe it is like never having read Shakespeare
Arthur Eddington: it holds “the supreme position among the laws of Nature”; he called its one-way direction the “arrow of time”
Ludwig Boltzmann explained it with statistics: disordered arrangements vastly outnumber orderly ones
Clausius (1865), the year he named entropy: the energy of the universe is constant, and its entropy tends toward a maximum
Gas let into an empty box spreads through both boxes and never squeezes itself back into one; the odds are far too tiny
Best possible engine efficiency: one minus the cold temperature divided by the hot temperature, both in kelvins
Living things obey it by raising their surroundings’ disorder; Schrödinger’s 1944 book _What Is Life?_ explored this
Max Planck wrote his 1879 doctoral thesis on it
Jacob Bekenstein proposed a “generalized” version that also counts the entropy of black holes
In Isaac Asimov’s 1956 story “The Last Question,” people keep asking ever more powerful computers whether its effects on the universe can be undone
A ship powered only by pulling heat out of the ocean would obey the conservation of energy but break this law
A snowflake can grow into an orderly crystal because the heat it releases raises the surrounding air’s disorder even more; a freezer making ice dumps heat into the kitchen

trap.title: The law, not entropy
trap.body: Entropy is a quantity (disorder, symbolized S), and the second law of thermodynamics is the rule that entropy never decreases in an isolated system. If a question asks for “this law,” saying only “entropy” is wrong; if it asks for “this quantity,” the answer is entropy. Players also mix up which numbered law is which, and saying just “second law” earns only a prompt, since Newton and Kepler have second laws too.
trap.fix: Energy being conserved is the first law; absolute zero and perfect crystals are the third law; thermometers and thermal equilibrium are the zeroth law. Heat flowing hot to cold, engines that can’t be 100 percent efficient, Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin, and Maxwell’s demon point to the second law. Say the whole name: “second law of thermodynamics.”
